articleBlocks: Fly and Cricket make this Pinpoint board feel slippery at the start because both words can point away from biology. Fly can be a verb, and Cricket can be a sport, so an early guess might chase motion, games, or summer activities. June beetle changes the tone because it is much harder to treat as anything except a creature name. Once that clue lands, the board asks for a tighter read of the first two clues.
The key move is to stop treating the clues as random nouns and ask whether every entry can work as a creature label.
Under that test, Fly is no longer an action word; it is the name of an insect.
Cricket stops being a sport clue and becomes the chirping insect.
June beetle, Praying mantis, and Lightning bug then keep the same kind of naming logic in place.
That makes Praying mantis the strongest turning clue, because it is specific enough to rule out the sports-and-motion read.
The board resolves because all five clues can be read as insect names without stretching any one clue.
solutionNarrative: I first tested the noisy readings because Fly and Cricket both invite them. Fly can sound like movement, and Cricket can sound like a game, so a loose summer or sports idea is tempting for a moment. June beetle made that path weaker, because it already behaves like a named bug rather than an activity or object.

The solve clicked when I used Praying mantis as the check clue. After that, I could go back through the board and read Fly as a fly, Cricket as a cricket, June beetle as a beetle, and Lightning bug as another familiar bug name. That was cleaner than any first guess, because it did not need a second meaning for the last three clues. The answer was "Names of insects".

lessons.title: "Lightning bug" confirms the final read without needing a second trick
